--- title: "Lecture 11 - Causal Inference Methods" subtitle: "ENCI707: Engineering Demand and Policy Analysis" footer: "[ENCI707 Home](/teaching/ENCI707/)" logo: "../../../assets/images/teaching/ENCI707/logo.png" format: revealjs: theme: simple transition: fade chalkboard: true slide-number: true execute: freeze: auto --- ## Learning Objectives ::: incremental 1. Understand why choice modellers should care about causal inference 2. Explain the three sources of causal identification 3. Connect causal identification sources to tools 4. Incorporate causal identification tools into choice model specifications ::: ## Why Choice Modellers Should Care About Causal Inference {.smaller} - Traditional choice studies estimate $$P(y_i=j|X_i)$$ - But policymakers usually ask ``what would happen if we changed X?" - This is a counterfactual question, not about prediction or goodness-of-fit - **Returning to our previous example:** People who like transit move near transit \& ride transit - We observe transit-proximate home choice \& transit use choice but the real story is **transit preference** ## Three Sources of Causal Identification {.smaller} 1. **Randomization** to create comparability - e.g., random treatment in DCE 2. **Statistical adjustment** to control for observed confounders - Matching - Propensity scores (PS) - Regression 3. **Natural experiments** by exploiting external variation - Instrumental variables (IV) - Difference-in-differences (DiD) - Regression discontinuity design (RDD) # Transportation Examples ## Propensity Score Matching for TOD Choice {.smaller} - **Policy question:** Does living near transit increase transit use? - **Problem:** People are not randomly assigned to neighbourhoods - **Matching on confounders:** Find people who are similar on income, household size, age, employment, and vehicle ownership but differ on transit proximity - **Option 1:** Estimate the model using a sample filtered to include only matched samples - **Option 2:** Use inverse propensity score weights directly in the choice model - i.e., $w_i = \frac{T_i}{e_i} + \frac{1-T_i}{1-e_i}$ where $e_i = P(T_i=1|X_i)$ ## IV for Residential Self-Selection {.smaller} - **Policy question:** Does living near transit increase transit use? - **Problem:** if $U_{Transit} = \beta N + \varepsilon$ where $N$ is a binary treatment for living near transit and we omit transit preference then $Cov(N,\varepsilon)\neq0$ - **IV solution:** use 2-stage control function estimation to adjust for endogeneity bias - $N = \pi Z + \nu$ where $Z$ is an instrument - e.g., historical streetcar network - $Z$ affects whether someone lives near transit today but does not directly affect current transit use - $U_{Transit} = \beta N + \lambda \hat{\nu} + \varepsilon$ - $\hat{\nu}$ is the residual part of residential location that could be related to transit preference ## DiD for New Rail Line {.smaller} - **Policy question:** Did a new rail line increase transit ridership? - **Problem:** need a counterfactual trend for before-after case - **DiD solution:** $U_{Transit,nt} = \beta X_{nt} + \delta (RailArea_n\times Post_t) + \varepsilon_{nt}$ - $\delta$ measures the DiD treatment effect - Requires panel data - Can include heterogeneity via $\delta_i$ and panel mixed logit model ## Mediation for Carbon Information->Attitude->Housing Downsizing {.smaller} - **Policy question:** Does information affect residential choice? - **Problem:** need to capture information->attitude connection - $U_{ni} = \beta Size_i + \gamma Carbon_i +\varepsilon_{ni}$ - Tells use whether carbon information matters but not why - **ICLV solution:** Mediation structure ```{mermaid} flowchart LR I["Carbon Information"] A["Environmental Concern"] D["Downsizing Choice"] I --> A A --> D ``` - Carbon information changes latent environmental concern, which changes residential preference ## Illustrating the 4 Methods :::{columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} #### PS ```{mermaid} %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontSize': '12px' }}}%% flowchart TB P["Income, Age,
Household Characteristics"] --> N["Transit Proximity"] P --> T["Transit Mode Choice"] N --> T ``` #### IV ```{mermaid} %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontSize': '12px' }}}%% flowchart LR Z["Streetcar
Network"] --> N["Lives Near
Transit"] N --> T["Transit Use"] V["Residual ν"] --> T ``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} #### DiD ```{mermaid} %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontSize': '12px' }}}%% flowchart TB T["Treatment
(Near Stations)"] --> B1["Before"] T --> A1["After"] C["Control
(Far Stations)"] --> B2["Before"] C --> A2["After"] ``` #### Mediation ICLV Model ```{mermaid} %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontSize': '12px' }}}%% flowchart LR I["Carbon Info"] --> A["Environmental
Concern"] A --> Q["Indicators
(Q1-Q3)"] A --> U["Downsizing
Utility"] --> C["Housing
Choice"] ``` ::: ::: # Supplemental Additional Details on Methods ## Propensity Score Matching (PSM) - **Matching**: restructure data for statistical analysis - Goal is to create attribute balance between treatment & control samples - Five step procedure ## PSM: Step 1 - Define confounders & estimand - Based on relevant literature - Typically adjust control group to match treated to estimate **effect of the treatment on the treated** - **Careful!** Including additional covariates may increase bias away from the true estimate if not all confounding covariates are available – avoid potential **instrumental variables** ## PSM: Step 2 - Estimating propensity score - Model of Pr(receiving treatment) - Typically, a **logistic regression** for binary treatment, then use propensity score as covariate summary - Propensity score gives a distance metric ## PSM: Step 3 - Matching to restructure data - Create matched pairs with control samples with closest propensity score – can be with/without replacement - Better matches with replacement but may overuse some sample units ## PSM: Step 4 - Diagnostics for balance & overlap - Several diagnostics exist based on difference of means, etc. - Evaluate and change model or method (if required) ## PSM: Step 5 - Estimate treatment effect using restructured data - Estimate regression model with propensity score and confounder variables - Incorporate data restructuring via **weights** – typically inverse probability weights ## Instrumental Variable (IV) - When ignorability of treatment seems weak, IV can be a good approach - Instrument $z$ should predict the treatment $T$ but not the outcome $y$ - Assumptions: - Ignorability of instrument - Monotonicity - Nonzero association between treatment & instrument - Exclusion restriction – no instrument effect on excluded variables ## IV in Regression - General framework $$𝑦_𝑖=\beta_0+\beta_1 𝑇_𝑖+\epsilon_𝑖$$ $$𝑇_𝑖=\gamma_0+\gamma_1 𝑧_𝑖+𝜈_𝑖$$ - Where $𝑧_𝑖$ is uncorrelated with both $\epsilon_𝑖$ and $𝜈_𝑖$ (ignorability and exclusion restriction) - **Identifiability**: whether data contain sufficient information for unique estimation of parameter (or set of parameters) ## IV in Regression {.smaller} - With $$𝑦=\beta_0+\beta_1 𝑇+\beta_2 𝑧+𝑒𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑟$$ $$𝑇=\gamma_0+\gamma_1 𝑧+𝑒𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑟$$ - Substituting $T$ into $y$: $$𝑦=(\beta_0+\beta_1 \gamma_0 )+(\beta_1 \gamma_1+\beta_2 )𝑧+𝑒𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑟$$ - where $\beta_1$ is our parameter of interest - Using $𝑦=\delta_0+\delta_1 𝑧+𝑒𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑟$ where $\delta_1=\beta_1 \gamma_1+\beta_2$ we get $$\beta_1=(\delta_1−\beta_2)/\gamma_1$$ ## IV in Regression - Cannot estimate $\beta_2$ because error in $f(y)$ can be correlated with T – exclusion restriction means $\beta_2=0$ giving $\beta_1=\delta_1/\gamma_1$ - Estimation is by two-stage least squares (2SLS) - Standard errors require adjustment in instrumental variable estimation – should be accounted for in any software package ## Exclusion Restriction Plausibility {.smaller} - One way to assess the plausibility of the exclusion restriction is to calculate an estimate within a sample that would not be expected to be affected by the instrument - Researchers estimated the effect of military service on earnings (and other outcomes) using, as an instrument, the lottery number for young men eligible for the draft during the Vietnam War - Randomly assigned number and strongly affected the probability of military service - Men with low lottery numbers may have altered their educational plans to avoid or postpone military service (would void exclusion restriction) - Ran IV model for a sample of men who were assigned numbers so late that the war ended before they ever had to serve - No clear relation between lottery number and earnings, providing support for the exclusion restriction ## Weak Instrument - Only assumption we can test – instrument has non-zero correlation with treatment variable - If low correlation, then a **weak instrument** ## Regression Discontinuity - **Non-random assignment** but **mechanism** entirely known to researcher - Consider a policy that gives tutoring to students with test scores < 60 - Consider all students with score in range of 60 – discontinuity at 60 - Works well when discontinuity relates to outcome – e.g., pre-test scores on post-test scores - Does not work well if comparing across **geography** due to spatial heterogeneity ## Fixed Effect Models - Use repeated observations within groups – e.g., twin comparisons that holds confounding variables fixed - Simply a regression model with group-specific intercepts $$𝑦_{𝑖𝑗}=\beta_0+\tau z_{𝑖𝑗}+\alpha_𝑖+\varepsilon_{𝑖𝑗}$$ - where $j$ is an indicator of intra-group units - Requires treatment to vary within groups ## Difference-In-Differences {.smaller} - Comparison across units (typically) using time as an additional dimension of variation - E.g., effect of new school busing program on housing prices in school district - Compare prices before/after between district with school busing program and those without it - A measure of **differences in trajectory** ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-11_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960} ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
